question: In which year was the First Battle of Panipat fought?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1526.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The First Battle of Panipat was fought on 21 April 1526 between Babur and Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan of the Lodi dynasty. Babur's victory founded the Mughal Empire in India. (पानीपत का प्रथम युद्ध — 1526)

 

• Babur won with a much smaller force by using two devices new to India:
◦ Field artillery, handled by his gunners Ustad Ali and Mustafa
◦ The Tulughma (flanking) tactic and the Araba formation, in which carts were lashed together to shield the guns

 

• Ibrahim Lodi was killed in the battle — the only Sultan of Delhi to die on the battlefield. Babur had been invited by Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor of Punjab, and Rana Sanga of Mewar.

 

• Babur wrote his memoirs, the "Tuzuk-i-Baburi" (Baburnama), in Chagatai Turki.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Babur's other major battles:
◦ Khanwa (1527) — against Rana Sanga of Mewar; Babur assumed the title Ghazi
◦ Chanderi (1528) — against Medini Rai
◦ Ghaghra (1529) — against the Afghans of Bihar and Bengal

 

• The three battles of Panipat: 1526 (Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi), 1556 (Akbar and Bairam Khan vs Hemu) and 1761 (Ahmad Shah Abdali vs the Marathas).

 

NOTE

 

• 1556 (Option 2): The Second Battle of Panipat, in which Akbar defeated Hemu.

 

• 1576 (Option 3): The year of the Battle of Haldighati, between Akbar's forces and Rana Pratap.

 

• 1761 (Option 4): The Third Battle of Panipat, in which the Marathas were defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali.

question: The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948 placed which of the following under the exclusive monopoly of the Central Government?
option_1: Coal, iron and steel and shipbuilding
option_2: Arms and ammunition, atomic energy and railway transport
option_4: Machine tools, fertilisers and heavy chemicals
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arms and ammunition, atomic energy and railway transport.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948, presented by Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee, was independent India's first industrial policy statement, and it established the framework of a mixed economy. (औद्योगिक नीति संकल्प 1948)

 

• It divided industries into four categories:
◦ Exclusive monopoly of the Central Government — arms and ammunition, atomic energy and railway transport
◦ New units to be set up only by the State — six industries including coal, iron and steel, aircraft manufacture, shipbuilding, telephone and telegraph equipment, and mineral oils; existing private units were allowed to continue for ten years
◦ Industries to be regulated by the Central Government — eighteen industries of national importance, such as automobiles, heavy chemicals, sugar, cement, cotton and woollen textiles
◦ All remaining industries — left to the private sector

 

• It was superseded by the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956, which divided industries into three schedules and is called the "Economic Constitution of India".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 gave the government the power of industrial licensing, which came to be known as the Licence Raj.

 

• The New Industrial Policy of 1991 abolished licensing for all but eighteen industries and reduced the industries reserved for the public sector from 17 to 8; at present only two remain — atomic energy and railway operations.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 names industries of the second category, in which new units were to be set up only by the State.

 

• Option 3 and Option 4 name industries of the third category, subject to central regulation but open to private enterprise.

question: The 'Dohas' of which saint-poet form an important part of the Nirguna Bhakti tradition?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kabir.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dohas (couplets) of Kabir are among the best-known compositions of the Nirguna Bhakti tradition, which worships a formless and attributeless God. (कबीर के दोहे — निर्गुण भक्ति परंपरा)

 

• Kabir (c. 1440-1518) was a weaver of Varanasi, and is said to have been a disciple of Ramananda. He rejected idol worship, caste distinctions, ritualism and the authority of both the Vedas and the Quran, and preached a religion of direct devotion.

 

• His verses are collected in the Bijak, and are known as Sakhi, Sabad and Ramaini. Some of his compositions are included in the Guru Granth Sahib. His followers are called Kabirpanthis.

 

• The Nirguna school also includes Guru Nanak, Dadu Dayal, Ravidas and Namdev; the Saguna school, which worships God with form and attributes, includes Tulsidas and Surdas (devotees of Rama and Krishna respectively), Mirabai and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Principal Bhakti saints and their regions: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), Madhvacharya (Dvaita), Ramananda (north India), Vallabhacharya (Pushtimarg), Chaitanya (Bengal), Namdev, Eknath and Tukaram (Maharashtra, the Varkari tradition), Shankaradeva (Assam) and the Alvars and Nayanars of the Tamil country.

 

• Guru Nanak (1469-1539), the founder of Sikhism, likewise emphasised one formless God, rejected idol worship and ritual, and instituted the langar.

 

NOTE

 

• Surdas (Option 2): A blind poet of the Saguna school, devoted to Krishna; author of the "Sursagar".

 

• Tulsidas (Option 3): Of the Saguna school; author of the "Ramcharitmanas" in Awadhi.

 

• Mirabai (Option 4): A Rajput princess and devotee of Krishna, belonging to the Saguna tradition.

question: The Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) was established in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1974.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) was incorporated on 24 January 1973 and began functioning as a holding company from 1974, when the management of the public sector steel plants was transferred to it. (सेल — 1974)

 

• It is one of India's largest steel producers and holds Maharatna status, conferred in 2010. Its headquarters is at New Delhi.

 

• Its integrated steel plants are at Bhilai (Chhattisgarh), Rourkela (Odisha), Durgapur and Burnpur/IISCO (West Bengal) and Bokaro (Jharkhand). The first three were set up during the Second Five Year Plan with Soviet, West German and British collaboration respectively.

 

• Its special steel plants are at Salem, Durgapur and Bhadravati.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's first modern steel plant was set up by Jamshedji Tata at Sakchi, now Jamshedpur, in 1907, as the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO).

 

• India is the second largest producer of crude steel in the world after China. The National Steel Policy 2017 targets a capacity of 300 million tonnes by 2030-31.

 

• Other Maharatna companies include ONGC, IOCL, NTPC, BHEL, GAIL, Coal India, BPCL, HPCL and Power Grid.

 

NOTE

 

• 1954 (Option 1) and 1964 (Option 2) are incorrect. Note that 1964 is the year the Unit Trust of India was established.

 

• 1984 (Option 4) is incorrect; SAIL was already a decade old by then.

question: The Kalinga War fought by Ashoka took place in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 261 BCE.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kalinga War was fought in 261 BCE, in the eighth year of Ashoka's reign, and is described in his Major Rock Edict XIII. (कलिंग युद्ध — 261 ईसा पूर्व)

 

• The edict records that one lakh people were killed, one and a half lakh were deported, and many times that number perished afterwards. The suffering caused by the war led Ashoka to renounce war altogether and to adopt Dhamma-vijaya, conquest through righteousness, in place of Digvijaya, conquest by arms.

 

• It is the only war Ashoka ever fought, and the only ancient inscription in the world in which a victorious king expresses remorse for his own victory. After it he was drawn to Buddhism, in which he was influenced by the monk Upagupta.

 

• Ashoka appointed Dhamma Mahamattas to propagate his ethical code, and sent missions abroad — his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra were sent to Sri Lanka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Key Mauryan dates: 321 BCE — Chandragupta Maurya founds the empire; 305 BCE — his conflict with Seleucus Nicator, followed by a treaty; 273 BCE — Ashoka's accession (he was formally crowned in 269 BCE); 232 BCE — Ashoka's death; 185 BCE — Brihadratha, the last Mauryan, killed by Pushyamitra Shunga.

 

• Ashoka's inscriptions were engraved in the Brahmi script over most of the empire, in Kharosthi in the north-west, and in Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar. They were deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837.

 

NOTE

 

• 305 BCE (Option 1): The approximate date of Chandragupta Maurya's conflict with Seleucus Nicator.

 

• 273 BCE (Option 2): The year of Ashoka's accession to the throne.

 

• 232 BCE (Option 4): The year of Ashoka's death.

question: In the human digestive system, the digestion of starch begins in which part?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mouth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The digestion of starch (carbohydrate) begins in the mouth (buccal cavity), where the enzyme salivary amylase (ptyalin), present in saliva, breaks starch down into simpler sugars. (स्टार्च का पाचन — मुख गुहा से आरंभ)

 

• Saliva is secreted by three pairs of salivary glands — the parotid, submandibular and sublingual. It is slightly alkaline, and about 1 to 1.5 litres is produced in a day.

 

• Where the digestion of each nutrient begins:
◦ Carbohydrate (starch) — in the mouth, by salivary amylase
◦ Protein — in the stomach, by pepsin acting in an acidic medium
◦ Fat — in the small intestine, by lipase, after bile has emulsified it

 

• The small intestine is where digestion is completed and where most absorption takes place, through the villi; the large intestine absorbs chiefly water and salts.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Digestive enzymes and their action:
◦ Salivary amylase — starch to maltose
◦ Pepsin — proteins to peptones; Rennin — curdles milk protein in infants
◦ Trypsin — proteins to peptides; Pancreatic amylase — starch to maltose; Lipase — fats to fatty acids and glycerol
◦ Maltase, sucrase, lactase — disaccharides to monosaccharides in the small intestine

 

• The liver is the largest gland in the body and secretes bile, which contains no enzyme but emulsifies fat and neutralises the acidic chyme.

 

NOTE

 

• Stomach (Option 2): Where protein digestion begins; salivary amylase is in fact inactivated here by the acidic medium.

 

• Small intestine (Option 3): Where digestion is completed and most absorption occurs.

 

• Large intestine (Option 4): Absorbs water and forms faeces; no digestion of starch occurs here.

question: The Buddhist doctrine of 'Pratityasamutpada' refers to which of the following?
option_1: The theory of many-sidedness of truth
solution_text:
The correct answer is The law of dependent origination.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Pratityasamutpada is the Buddhist law of dependent origination, which holds that every phenomenon arises in dependence upon causes and conditions, and that nothing exists independently or eternally. (प्रतीत्यसमुत्पाद — कार्य-कारण का सिद्धांत)

 

• It is often summed up in the formula: *"This being, that becomes; from the arising of this, that arises."* From it follow the two other central Buddhist doctrines:
◦ Anitya (impermanence) — since everything is conditioned, nothing is permanent
◦ Anatta (no-self) — there is no unchanging soul, only a stream of conditioned states

 

• The doctrine is set out as a chain of twelve links (Dvadasha Nidana), beginning with ignorance (avidya) and ending with old age and death, and it explains how suffering arises and how, by removing its cause, it may be ended.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Four Noble Truths — Dukkha, Samudaya, Nirodha and Magga — and the Eightfold Path were preached in the Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath.

 

• The Eightfold Path consists of Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration. It is called the Madhyama Pratipada, or Middle Path, between extreme indulgence and extreme austerity.

 

• Buddhist scriptures, the Tripitakas, are in Pali; Buddhism split into Hinayana and Mahayana at the Fourth Council under Kanishka.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 describes the Jaina doctrines of Anekantavada and Syadvada, the theory of the many-sidedness of truth.

 

• Option 2 describes Ahimsa, central to both Buddhism and Jainism but not the meaning of this term.

 

• Option 4 describes the Vedic Yajna, which the Buddha expressly rejected.

question: The deficiency of which hormone causes diabetes mellitus in human beings?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Insulin.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Diabetes mellitus is caused by a deficiency of the hormone insulin, or by the body's inability to use it properly. (मधुमेह — इंसुलिन की कमी)

 

• Insulin is secreted by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It lowers the level of glucose in the blood by promoting its uptake by the cells and its storage as glycogen in the liver.

 

• Its antagonist is glucagon, secreted by the alpha cells, which raises blood glucose. The two together maintain the balance of blood sugar.

 

• Insulin was discovered by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in 1921, for which Banting shared the Nobel Prize in 1923.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Hormones, their glands and the disorders of deficiency or excess:
◦ Thyroxine — thyroid; deficiency causes goitre and cretinism in children, myxoedema in adults; excess causes Grave's disease. Its production requires iodine.
◦ Growth hormone — pituitary; deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism, excess causes gigantism, and excess in adulthood causes acromegaly
◦ Adrenaline — adrenal medulla; the emergency hormone, secreted in fear, fight and flight
◦ Parathormone — parathyroid; regulates calcium and phosphorus

 

• The pituitary is called the master gland, and the pancreas is a dual gland, both exocrine and endocrine.

 

NOTE

 

• Adrenaline (Option 1): Prepares the body for emergencies; it raises blood sugar but its deficiency does not cause diabetes.

 

• Thyroxine (Option 2): Its deficiency causes goitre, not diabetes.

 

• Growth hormone (Option 4): Its deficiency in childhood causes dwarfism.

 

• Note also diabetes insipidus, a different disorder caused by a deficiency of the antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin).

question: The 'Losoong' festival, which marks the end of the harvest season, is celebrated chiefly in which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sikkim.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Losoong, also called Namsoong among the Lepchas, is celebrated chiefly in Sikkim to mark the end of the harvest season and the close of the Tibetan lunar year. (लोसूंग — सिक्किम)

 

• It falls in the tenth month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in December, and is observed by both the Bhutia and Lepcha communities. Its principal attraction is the Chaam masked dance performed by lamas at the Rumtek, Phodong and Tsuklakhang monasteries, which is believed to drive away evil spirits of the outgoing year.

 

• Other festivals of Sikkim: Pang Lhabsol, in honour of Mount Khangchendzonga as the guardian deity; Saga Dawa, marking the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha; Bhumchu at the Tashiding monastery; and Maghe Sankranti.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harvest festivals of India frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Baisakhi — Punjab; Bihu — Assam; Pongal — Tamil Nadu
◦ Onam — Kerala; Nuakhai — Odisha; Wangala — Meghalaya (Garo)
◦ Makar Sankranti — much of northern India; Lohri — Punjab
◦ Ka Pomblang Nongkrem — Meghalaya (Khasi); Ka Shad Suk Mynsiem — Meghalaya

 

• Sikkim became the 22nd state of India in 1975. Khangchendzonga National Park is India's only mixed UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016.

 

NOTE

 

• Himachal Pradesh (Option 1): Celebrates Kullu Dussehra, Losar in Lahaul-Spiti and the Minjar Fair.

 

• Ladakh (Option 2): Celebrates Losar, Dosmoche and the Hemis Festival.

 

• Arunachal Pradesh (Option 3): Celebrates Losar, Solung, Mopin and Nyokum.

question: Wood's Despatch of 1854, regarded as the 'Magna Carta of English education in India', was issued during the tenure of which Governor-General?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Dalhousie.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Wood's Despatch of 1854 was issued during the tenure of Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856), and is called the "Magna Carta of English education in India". It was sent by Sir Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control. (वुड का घोषणापत्र, 1854)

 

• Its principal recommendations:
◦ The establishment of universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, on the model of the University of London — set up in 1857
◦ A Department of Public Instruction in each of the five provinces
◦ A graded system of schools — vernacular primary schools, Anglo-vernacular high schools and affiliated colleges
◦ English as the medium of instruction at the higher stages and the vernaculars at the lower
◦ Grants-in-aid to private schools, and the promotion of women's education and vocational and teacher training

 

• Lord Dalhousie is also remembered for the Doctrine of Lapse, the introduction of the railways (1853), the telegraph and the postal reforms of 1854.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Landmarks in colonial education:
◦ Macaulay's Minute (1835) and the English Education Act, under Lord William Bentinck, which settled the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy in favour of English
◦ Wood's Despatch (1854) — under Dalhousie
◦ Hunter Commission (1882) — under Lord Ripon, on primary and secondary education
◦ Indian Universities Act (1904) — under Lord Curzon
◦ Sadler Commission (1917) and the Hartog Committee (1929)

 

NOTE

 

• Lord William Bentinck (Option 1): Associated with Macaulay's Minute of 1835 and the abolition of Sati in 1829.

 

• Lord Ripon (Option 2): Appointed the Hunter Commission and is known for local self-government and the Ilbert Bill.

 

• Lord Curzon (Option 3): Passed the Indian Universities Act, 1904 and partitioned Bengal in 1905.

question: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Coulomb.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C), named after the French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb. (विद्युत आवेश का मात्रक — कूलॉम)

 

• One coulomb is the quantity of charge that passes a point in a conductor when a current of one ampere flows for one second:
◦ Q = I × t, so 1 C = 1 A × 1 s

 

• The charge on a single electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb, so one coulomb is the charge of about 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

 

• Coulomb's Law states that the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = kq₁q₂ / r².

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Electrical quantities and their SI units:
◦ Current — ampere (A), a base SI unit
◦ Charge — coulomb (C)
◦ Potential difference / voltage — volt (V)
◦ Resistance — ohm (Ω); Resistivity — ohm-metre
◦ Power — watt (W); Energy — joule (J)
◦ Capacitance — farad (F); Inductance — henry (H)
◦ Magnetic flux — weber (Wb); Magnetic flux density — tesla (T)

 

• Ohm's Law states that V = IR, provided the physical conditions remain constant.

 

NOTE

 

• Ampere (Option 1): The SI unit of electric current, and one of the seven base units.

 

• Volt (Option 3): The SI unit of potential difference.

 

• Ohm (Option 4): The SI unit of electrical resistance.

question: 'Kajari', a folk song traditionally sung during the rainy season, is associated with which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uttar Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kajari (also Kajri) is a folk song of the rainy season, sung chiefly in Uttar Pradesh, particularly in the Mirzapur, Varanasi and Bhojpur regions, and also in parts of Bihar. (कजरी — उत्तर प्रदेश)

 

• It is sung in the month of Sawan (Bhadrapada), especially around Kajari Teej, and its themes are the longing of a wife for her husband who is away, and the joy of the monsoon.

 

• It is traditionally sung by women in groups, and Mirzapur is regarded as its principal home. In classical music it is counted among the semi-classical (upashastriya) forms, along with Thumri, Dadra, Chaiti and Hori.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Folk songs of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, and their occasions:
◦ Sohar — the birth of a child
◦ Kajari — the rainy season
◦ Chaiti — the month of Chaitra
◦ Hori — the festival of Holi
◦ Birha — songs of separation, associated with the Ahirs
◦ Alha — heroic ballads of Alha and Udal
◦ Barahmasa — songs of the twelve months
◦ Vidaai / Banna-Banni — marriage songs

 

• Folk songs of other states: Mand and Pankhida (Rajasthan), Powada and Lavani (Maharashtra), Baul (West Bengal), Heer and Tappa (Punjab), Mando (Goa), Pandavani (Chhattisgarh) and Wanawan (Jammu & Kashmir).

 

NOTE

 

• Odisha (Option 1): Known for Dalkhai and the devotional songs of the Jagannath tradition.

 

• Punjab (Option 2): Known for Heer, Mahiya, Tappa and Boliyan.

 

• Gujarat (Option 3): Known for Garba geet and Dayro.

question: Who founded the 'Satyashodhak Samaj' in 1873?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jyotiba Phule.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Satyashodhak Samaj (Society of Truth Seekers) was founded on 24 September 1873 at Pune by Jyotiba Phule. (सत्यशोधक समाज — ज्योतिबा फुले, 1873)

 

• Its aims were to liberate the Shudras and Ati-Shudras from the domination of the Brahmanas, to end the exploitation of the lower castes and to secure them education and equal rights. It encouraged marriages performed without Brahmana priests.

 

• Phule opened the first school for girls in India at Pune in 1848, and a school for the children of untouchables, in which his wife Savitribai Phule — regarded as India's first woman teacher — taught. He also opened a home for widows and for the prevention of infanticide.

 

• His principal works are "Gulamgiri" (Slavery, 1873) and "Shetkaryacha Asud" (The Cultivator's Whipcord). He was given the title "Mahatma" in 1888.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other social reform movements and their founders:
◦ Brahmo Samaj (1828) — Raja Rammohan Roy
◦ Arya Samaj (1875) — Swami Dayanand Saraswati
◦ Prarthana Samaj (1867) — Atmaram Pandurang
◦ Ramakrishna Mission (1897) — Swami Vivekananda
◦ SNDP Yogam (1903) — Sree Narayana Guru, in Kerala; his motto was *"One caste, one religion, one God for man"*
◦ Self-Respect Movement (1925) — Periyar E.V. Ramasamy, in Tamil Nadu
◦ Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) and the Depressed Classes Federation — Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

 

NOTE

 

• Periyar (Option 1): Founded the Self-Respect Movement in Tamil Nadu in 1925.

 

• B.R. Ambedkar (Option 2): Founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha in 1924 and led the Mahad Satyagraha in 1927; he was born much later than 1873.

 

• Narayana Guru (Option 3): The Kerala reformer who founded the SNDP Yogam in 1903.

question: Which Indian city hosted the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence (GPAI) Summit in December 2023?
solution_text:
The correct answer is New Delhi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence (GPAI) Summit was hosted by India at New Delhi from 12 to 14 December 2023, at Bharat Mandapam. (जीपीएआई शिखर सम्मेलन — नई दिल्ली, दिसंबर 2023)

 

• India held the Chair of GPAI for 2024, taking over from Japan. The summit adopted the New Delhi Declaration, which stressed safe, secure and trustworthy AI, equitable access, and the use of AI for the Sustainable Development Goals.

 

• GPAI was launched in June 2020 as a multi-stakeholder international initiative to bridge the gap between theory and practice in artificial intelligence. India is a founding member, and the OECD provides its secretariat.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's AI initiatives: the IndiaAI Mission, approved in 2024 to build computing capacity, datasets and skills; BharatGen, the first government-funded multimodal large language model; Bhashini, the National Language Translation Mission; and the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (#AIforAll) published by NITI Aayog in 2018.

 

• Other major summits hosted by India: the G20 Summit at New Delhi in September 2023, under the theme "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — One Earth, One Family, One Future", at which the African Union was admitted as a permanent member.

 

NOTE

 

• Mumbai (Option 1): Hosted the World Economic Forum India Economic Summit in earlier years.

 

• Bengaluru (Option 2): India's principal technology hub and the venue of the Bengaluru Tech Summit and Aero India, but not of the GPAI Summit.

 

• Hyderabad (Option 3): Hosted the World Congress on Information Technology in 2018.

question: Which of the following was NOT a component of the New Economic Policy adopted by India in 1991?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nationalisation of commercial banks.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The New Economic Policy of 1991 rested on three components — Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation (LPG). The nationalisation of commercial banks was no part of it; on the contrary, it belonged to an earlier and opposite phase of economic policy. (एलपीजी सुधार — बैंक राष्ट्रीयकरण इसका भाग नहीं)

 

• Banks were nationalised in 1969 (14 banks) and again in 1980 (6 banks), more than two decades before the reforms. The 1991 policy moved in the reverse direction, opening banking to private and foreign participation on the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee (1991).

 

• The three components in brief:
◦ Liberalisation — abolition of industrial licensing for most industries, removal of the MRTP asset limit, deregulation of interest rates
◦ Privatisation — disinvestment in public sector enterprises, and reduction of the industries reserved for the public sector from 17 to 8
◦ Globalisation — reduction of tariffs, removal of quantitative restrictions, devaluation of the rupee and liberalised foreign direct investment

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The reforms were introduced under Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh, in response to a balance of payments crisis in which foreign exchange reserves had fallen to about two weeks' worth of imports.

 

• Accompanying measures included a loan from the IMF, the abolition of the Controller of Capital Issues, statutory status for SEBI in 1992, and tax reforms on the recommendations of the Chelliah Committee.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 are the three pillars of the 1991 policy, and are commonly remembered together by the abbreviation LPG.

question: What is the name of India's first indigenously developed vaccine against cervical cancer, launched in 2022?
solution_text:
The correct answer is CERVAVAC.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• CERVAVAC is India's first indigenously developed vaccine against cervical cancer, launched in 2022. It is a quadrivalent Human Papillomavirus (qHPV) vaccine. (सर्वावैक — भारत का पहला स्वदेशी सर्वाइकल कैंसर टीका)

 

• It was developed by the Serum Institute of India, Pune, with support from the Department of Biotechnology and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC). It received approval from the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) in July 2022.

 

• It protects against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18; types 16 and 18 are responsible for the large majority of cervical cancers.

 

• Cervical cancer is among the commonest cancers among women in India. The vaccine is intended chiefly for girls aged 9 to 14 years, before exposure to the virus.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other vaccines developed in India:
◦ Covaxin (BBV152) — India's first indigenous COVID-19 vaccine, by Bharat Biotech with the ICMR; an inactivated virus vaccine
◦ ZyCoV-D — by Zydus Cadila; the world's first DNA plasmid-based COVID-19 vaccine, administered needle-free
◦ Corbevax — by Biological E; a protein subunit vaccine
◦ iNCOVACC — the world's first intranasal COVID-19 vaccine
◦ Rotavac — against rotavirus diarrhoea, developed indigenously

 

• The Serum Institute of India is the world's largest vaccine manufacturer by volume.

 

NOTE

 

• Corbevax (Option 1): A protein subunit COVID-19 vaccine.

 

• ZyCoV-D (Option 2): The world's first DNA-based COVID-19 vaccine, not a cancer vaccine.

 

• Covaxin (Option 3): India's first indigenous COVID-19 vaccine.

question: Which of the following is a Kharif crop?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rice.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rice is a Kharif crop. Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon in June-July and harvested in September-October. (खरीफ फसल — धान)

 

• The three cropping seasons of India:
◦ Kharif (June-July to September-October) — rice, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, cotton, jute, groundnut, soybean, tur (arhar), sugarcane
◦ Rabi (October-November to March-April) — wheat, barley, gram, peas, mustard, linseed
◦ Zaid (March-April to June) — watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder crops

 

• Rice requires high temperature (above 25°C), high humidity and rainfall above 100 cm, and is grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, the coastal areas and the deltaic regions. West Bengal is the largest producer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wheat is the second most important cereal of India, requiring a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of ripening. Uttar Pradesh is the largest producer, and the Green Revolution of the 1960s greatly raised its yield in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Plantation crops — tea, coffee, rubber, coconut, spices — are grown on estates, are capital and labour intensive, and are chiefly grown for the market.

 

• M.S. Swaminathan is called the Father of the Green Revolution in India, and Norman Borlaug the Father of the Green Revolution worldwide.

 

NOTE

 

• Wheat (Option 1), Barley (Option 2) and Mustard (Option 4) are all Rabi crops, sown in winter and harvested in spring.

question: Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is calculated at ______.
option_2: constant prices of a base year
option_3: prices fixed by the Reserve Bank of India
solution_text:
The correct answer is constant prices of a base year.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Real GDP is calculated at the constant prices of a chosen base year, so that the effect of price changes is removed and only the change in the volume of output is measured. (वास्तविक जीडीपी — स्थिर कीमतों पर)

 

• Nominal GDP, by contrast, is calculated at current prices, and therefore rises both when output increases and when prices increase. Real GDP is thus the better measure of genuine economic growth.

 

• The relation between the two is given by the GDP Deflator:
◦ GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100
◦ It is a comprehensive measure of the general price level in an economy.

 

• In India, national income is estimated by the National Statistical Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, and the present base year is 2011-12.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Key national income relationships:
◦ GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad
◦ NDP = GDP − Depreciation; NNP = GNP − Depreciation
◦ National Income = NNP at factor cost = NNP at market price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies

 

• Dadabhai Naoroji made the first estimate of India's national income in "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India", and the first scientific estimate after Independence was made by the National Income Committee (1949) under P.C. Mahalanobis.

 

NOTE

 

• Current prevailing prices (Option 1): The basis of Nominal GDP, not Real GDP — the commonest confusion in this question.

 

• Options 3 and 4 are incorrect; neither the Reserve Bank nor international markets fix the prices used in national income accounting.

question: Which of the following statements about inflation is INCORRECT?
option_1: Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money.
option_2: Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply.
option_3: Cost-push inflation arises from a rise in the cost of production.
option_4: Inflation benefits creditors and harms debtors.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Inflation benefits creditors and harms debtors.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This statement is INCORRECT, because the effect is exactly the reverse: inflation benefits debtors and harms creditors. (मुद्रास्फीति से ऋणी को लाभ और ऋणदाता को हानि)

 

• The reason is that a debtor repays a fixed sum of money whose real value has fallen by the time of repayment. The creditor receives the same number of rupees, but those rupees buy less than they did when the loan was made.

 

• The other three statements are correct:
◦ Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money — this is the very definition of inflation.
◦ Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply at the existing price level — "too much money chasing too few goods".
◦ Cost-push inflation arises from a rise in the cost of production, such as higher wages or higher prices of raw materials and fuel.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Types of inflation by rate: Creeping (up to 3%), Walking (3-7%), Running (10-20%), Galloping (20-100%) and Hyperinflation (extremely rapid, as in Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in 2008).

 

• Related terms: Deflation (a general fall in prices), Disinflation (a fall in the rate of inflation), Stagflation (inflation together with stagnation and unemployment) and Reflation.

 

• Who gains and who loses: debtors, producers and those holding real assets gain; creditors, pensioners, wage earners on fixed salaries and holders of cash lose.

 

• India's inflation target is 4% with a tolerance band of ±2%, measured by the Consumer Price Index (Combined).

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 3 are all correct statements about inflation, and are therefore not the answer to a question asking for the incorrect one.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding groundwater resources in India?

I. Punjab and Haryana have very high levels of groundwater utilisation.

II. Groundwater is a renewable resource.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. (भूजल — पंजाब एवं हरियाणा में अत्यधिक दोहन; भूजल एक नवीकरणीय संसाधन)

 

• Statement I is correct: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu utilise a very large proportion of their groundwater resources, in several districts exceeding the annually replenishable quantity. This is chiefly the result of intensive tube-well irrigation for water-demanding crops such as rice and wheat, encouraged by subsidised power.

 

• Statement II is correct: groundwater is a renewable resource, replenished each year by the percolation of rainfall and surface water. It ceases to be sustainable only when the rate of extraction exceeds the rate of recharge, which is the condition described as over-exploitation.

 

• The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, assesses groundwater and classifies assessment units as safe, semi-critical, critical or over-exploited.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• India is the largest user of groundwater in the world, drawing more than the United States and China together. About 60% of irrigation and 85% of rural drinking water depend on it.

 

• Measures for conservation: rainwater harvesting, the Atal Bhujal Yojana, the Jal Shakti Abhiyan, watershed development, micro-irrigation (drip and sprinkler) and the promotion of less water-intensive crops.

 

• Constraints on the use of surface water in India include the topography, the seasonal and uneven distribution of rainfall, and pollution.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: Who is the author of the novel 'Nectar in a Sieve'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kamala Markandaya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Nectar in a Sieve" (1954) was written by Kamala Markandaya. It was her first published novel and remains her best known. (नेक्टर इन ए सीव — कमला मार्कण्डेय)

 

• The novel is narrated by Rukmani, a peasant woman, and describes the destruction of village life by famine, land loss and the coming of a tannery. Its title is taken from a line of Coleridge: *"Work without hope draws nectar in a sieve."*

 

• Her other novels include "Some Inner Fury", "A Silence of Desire", "A Handful of Rice" and "The Nowhere Man".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Indian women writers in English and their principal works:
◦ Anita Desai — *Clear Light of Day*, *In Custody*, *Fire on the Mountain*; shortlisted for the Booker three times
◦ Kamala Das (Madhavikutty) — *My Story*, *Summer in Calcutta*; wrote in both English and Malayalam
◦ Nayantara Sahgal — *Rich Like Us*, which won the Sahitya Akademi Award
◦ Arundhati Roy — *The God of Small Things*, Booker Prize 1997
◦ Kiran Desai — *The Inheritance of Loss*, Booker Prize 2006
◦ Jhumpa Lahiri — *Interpreter of Maladies*, Pulitzer Prize 2000
◦ Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni — *The Palace of Illusions*

 

• Novels of rural and peasant life: "Untouchable" and "The Village" by Mulk Raj Anand, and "Kanthapura" by Raja Rao.

 

NOTE

 

• Nayantara Sahgal (Option 1): Author of "Rich Like Us"; she returned her Sahitya Akademi Award in 2015.

 

• Anita Desai (Option 2): Author of "In Custody", later filmed by Merchant Ivory.

 

• Kamala Das (Option 3): Best known for her autobiography "My Story" and her poetry.

question: In which year did India overtake the United Kingdom to become the fifth largest economy in the world by nominal GDP?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2022.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• India overtook the United Kingdom to become the fifth largest economy in the world by nominal GDP in 2022. (2022 — भारत विश्व की पाँचवीं सबसे बड़ी अर्थव्यवस्था)

 

• The four economies larger than India at that point were the United States, China, Japan and Germany.

 

• A distinction worth remembering: by nominal GDP India ranks fifth, but by GDP at Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) India has been the third largest economy for some years, after China and the United States. PPP adjusts for differences in the cost of living between countries.

 

• India's GDP crossed the one trillion dollar mark in 2007 and the two trillion dollar mark in 2014.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's economy is dominated by the services sector, which contributes roughly 55% of Gross Value Added, followed by industry and then agriculture. Agriculture, however, still supports the largest share of the workforce.

 

• National income in India is estimated by the National Statistical Office (NSO) under MoSPI, with 2011-12 as the base year.

 

• India is a member of the G20, and hosted its summit at New Delhi in September 2023.

 

NOTE

 

• 2018 (Option 1) and 2020 (Option 2) are too early; India was then ranked sixth or seventh by nominal GDP.

 

• 2024 (Option 4) is incorrect. Note that 2014 was the year India's GDP crossed two trillion dollars, which is a separate milestone often confused with this one.

question: The Sun Temple at Konark, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was built by which ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Narasimhadeva I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sun Temple at Konark in Odisha was built in the thirteenth century (c. 1250 CE) by King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. (कोणार्क सूर्य मंदिर — नरसिंहदेव प्रथम)

 

• The temple is conceived as the colossal chariot of the Sun God Surya, drawn by seven horses and mounted on twenty-four intricately carved stone wheels, each of which functions as a sundial.

 

• It is built in the Kalinga style of Nagara architecture, and European sailors called it the "Black Pagoda", as against the "White Pagoda" of the Jagannath temple at Puri. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.

 

• The main sanctuary (deul) has collapsed; what survives chiefly is the Jagamohana, the assembly hall.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other famous temples and their builders:
◦ Brihadeshwara Temple, Thanjavur — Rajaraja Chola I; a UNESCO site among the Great Living Chola Temples
◦ Khajuraho temples — the Chandela rulers
◦ Lingaraja Temple, Bhubaneswar — the Somavamshi dynasty
◦ Jagannath Temple, Puri — Anantavarman Chodaganga of the Eastern Ganga dynasty
◦ Kailasa Temple, Ellora — Krishna I of the Rashtrakutas
◦ Shore Temple, Mahabalipuram — the Pallavas, under Narasimhavarman II
◦ Dilwara Temples, Mount Abu — built under Solanki patronage
◦ Vitthala Temple, Hampi — the Vijayanagara rulers

 

NOTE

 

• Rajaraja Chola I (Option 2): Built the Brihadeshwara Temple at Thanjavur in 1010 CE.

 

• Krishnadevaraya (Option 3): The greatest Vijayanagara ruler, associated with the temples of Hampi.

 

• Mahendravarman I (Option 4): A Pallava ruler, associated with the early rock-cut cave temples of Tamil Nadu.

question: Which of the following is a macronutrient required by plants from the soil?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nitrogen.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nitrogen is a macronutrient — one of the elements that plants require in large quantities. (नाइट्रोजन — वृहत् पोषक तत्व)

 

• The sixteen essential nutrients for plants are divided as follows:
◦ Basic nutrients (from air and water) — carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
◦ Primary macronutrients — nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K); these are the three supplied by NPK fertilisers
◦ Secondary macronutrients — calcium, magnesium, sulphur
◦ Micronutrients (trace elements) — iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine

 

• The functions of nitrogen are central: it is a constituent of proteins, chlorophyll, nucleic acids and enzymes. Its deficiency causes chlorosis, the yellowing of leaves, and stunted growth.

 

• Nitrogen is fixed from the atmosphere by Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of leguminous plants such as gram, pea and groundnut, which is why such crops are used in crop rotation to restore soil fertility.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Deficiency symptoms worth remembering: nitrogen — chlorosis; phosphorus — poor root development and purplish leaves; potassium — scorched leaf margins; iron — chlorosis of young leaves; zinc — "little leaf" disease.

 

• Urea is the most widely used nitrogenous fertiliser in India, containing about 46% nitrogen.

 

NOTE

 

• Zinc (Option 1), Boron (Option 3) and Copper (Option 4) are all micronutrients, required by plants only in very small quantities, though they are equally essential.

question: In Hindustani classical music, which is the slow, elaborate opening section performed without rhythmic accompaniment?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Alap.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Alap is the slow, elaborate opening section of a Hindustani classical performance, in which the raga is unfolded note by note without any rhythmic accompaniment and without a fixed tala. (आलाप — बिना ताल का धीमा प्रारंभिक भाग)

 

• Its purpose is to establish the mood and the grammar of the raga — its ascending and descending scales (aroha and avaroha), its principal notes (vadi and samvadi) and its characteristic phrases. Only the tanpura provides a drone.

 

• The sections that follow in an instrumental performance:
◦ Jor — a pulse or steady rhythm begins, though still without the tabla
◦ Jhala — a fast, exciting concluding passage played with rapid strokes
◦ Gat — the composition proper, with tabla accompaniment
◦ Taan — rapid runs of notes woven into the performance to display virtuosity

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dhrupad is the oldest surviving form of Hindustani vocal music, austere and devotional in character. Khayal is the dominant modern form, and the semi-classical forms include Thumri, Dadra, Tappa, Kajari and Chaiti.

 

• Basic terms: Raga (the melodic framework), Tala (the rhythmic cycle), Swara (note), Sthayi and Antara (sections of a composition), and Gharana (a school or lineage).

 

• The main gharanas of Hindustani music are Gwalior (the oldest), Agra, Jaipur-Atrauli, Kirana, Patiala and Rampur-Sahaswan.

 

NOTE

 

• Jor (Option 2): Follows the alap, when a steady pulse enters, but still without percussion.

 

• Jhala (Option 3): The rapid, climactic concluding section.

 

• Taan (Option 4): A fast melodic run used within a performance, not an opening section.
